utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. My apologies. I was distracted by another matter and has meant being a little late starting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Would I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth. That still applies. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 02229 back up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday when we left off we were -- you were describing this sketch that you had drawn, and I had asked you about the numbers that were marked as 1 through 4. We see now the whole sketch and there's a legend at the bottom. Was this legend also prepared by yourself?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could zoom in in the section of the legend to the numbers 1 through 6. And if you could read out the names that you have marked as numbers 1 through 6 here in the legend.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, Cvetan Sasa; number 2, Borojevic Dragan, aka Rodja; number 3, Dragan Medic, aka Gulja; number 4, Demirovic, I didn't know his first name at the time, but I know now it is Dejan; number 5, unknown, a police officer in blue uniform; and number 6, Solaja Miodrag aka Zicko.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There are two other names we see, there's Smiljic Zdravko and Dabic Sasa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could zoom out of the legend, back into, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see that you've marked these two persons being something up on what you marked a terrace. Would these two persons have been persons who had in your opinion been able to observe the incident that took place in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my opinion, although they refuted that before a court in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned when you were reading out the names -- the name of Dragan Medic. Could you tell us who he was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Medic, in a previous composition of the Skorpions, i.e., before the events in Kosovo and the time of preordered agreement, he was the commander of a Skorpion company. Namely, the Skorpions were comprised of two companies. One recognisance platoon and one working platoon. He was the commander of the first company.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And with regard to the persons that you just read out the names you just read out that you have indicated you saw in the courtyard, would Mr. Medic, Dragan Medic, have been someone of the same rank as those persons or of a higher rank as those persons whose names you just read out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I cannot be absolutely certain, but I do believe that he had issued an order for these civilians to be executed for the simple reason that he had the highest rank among this group. It would be foolish for someone with a lower rank to issue such an order if there was a person that had a higher rank than this one. Therefore, I presume that he was the one who gave the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence. It's 02229.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00498, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you arrived in the courtyard and saw these persons there and saw the civilians, were you able to ask anyone who was there what had happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I managed to take a look for what -- about 20 or 30 seconds. I didn't ask anyone anything. It was clear to me that the women and the children that I had seen in the street and who returned into the courtyard, it was clear to me that they had been shot at. We all somehow went out into the street of our own accord. I didn't ask anyone at the moment. Only later when we boarded the buses, I started asking questions about the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what were you told when you were on the bus and you started asking questions about the event?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we went on the bus there was a small detail that left a huge impression on me, and that was the line-up before the buses arrived. While we were lined up, an officer, Tutinac or Zoran Simovic, came. I never felt more humiliated in my life than after he had delivered his speech. He used very harsh words to criticise us; he used very abusive language. "You pigs. No one can work with you. What have you done?" At that moment the buses arrived, and he ordered us to board them. Of course, before Mr. Tutinac, Dr. Dragan came with a few number of the active officers of the SAJ. I cannot tell you their real names because they all had code-names due to the specific nature of their work such as Vuk, Strela, Top, et cetera. I remember a name who was called Vuk. He was helping the doctor to carry out, either in a blanket or in some other items, they were carrying children to the ambulance. So this all happened, and I saw all this within the span of ten minutes. The first one to react on the bus was Zeljko Djukic aka Brka, he was sitting next to the driver. He got up and he said, although I wouldn't like to quote him, but he said something to the effect that only a fool could have done this. I myself have three --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to slow down and repeat the last portion of his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you mind just repeating. You were telling us that Djukic had said something to the effect that only a fool could have done this what you're saying after this I myself have three something, and the interpreters didn't catch what you said. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zeljko Djukic got up, turned toward the soldiers and said, "Only a fool could have done this. I myself have three children." He obviously didn't agree with what had happened. After that, Dragan Medic got up, who had the highest rank in the group, and he said, "Shut up, Brka. I did it. So what?" And in front of all of us he publicly admitted to this. After that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, may I just stop you there. You had mentioned the name of Mr. Tutinac when you were speaking about what happened immediately after the incident. Could you remind us who he was, Mr. Tutinac who you referred to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tutinac, I think his real name is Zoran Simovic, was a high-ranking officer of the SAJ. Believe me, I thought that he was going to shoot us dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. In your statement, you indicate that you were put on these buses and that you were describing and that you were driven back or sent back to Prolom Banja. In total, how much time did you end up spending in Podujevo before being sent back to Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little time. I think less than one hour. However, I have to tell you, when we board the buses and returned to Prolom Banja, one of our platoons got lost and everybody forgot about it. They stayed in Podujevo the whole night. Only the next morning were they returned to Prolom Banja. Therefore, I believe that I didn't stay there longer than one hour. But it couldn't be or shouldn't be correct. It could be one and a half hours, could be half an hour. I cannot say exactly had. But on this street and this yard; and before I saw the civilians and when they arrived and then sent out into the street, the total time I spent there was about 15 minutes in the courtyard and in the house marked A and highlighted yellow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when you were sent back to Prolom Banja did you expect some sort of punishment for what had happened in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, a coup let's call it that, took place in Prolom Banja. Namely, according to my estimate, 30 per cent of the soldiers, members of the unit, wanted immediately to be released and sent home from Kosovo. Nebojsa Cekic of Nis personally gave me his weapon and said, "Give my rifle back to the commander. I didn't come here to kill children." Since Prolom Banja and Nis are not far apart, so he somehow managed to leave the unit on his own. He gave me his rifle to return it to the commander precisely because on his arrival in Prolom Banja I called him myself and I mobilised him to come to Prolom Banja. So this coup took place, and it took a lot of effort to get a bus from Medic for the man who didn't want to stay any longer there and who wanted to return to Serbia. He delivered a speech. He lined us all up in order to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I'm just going to stop you there so we can -- because this is in your statement. Was anyone questioned about the indent that happened at Podujevo when you returned to Prolom Banja? For example, were you questioned about what happen in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of that, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was anyone in the group arrested or taken into custody because of the indent that happened at Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, after the signing of the Kumanovo Agreement and the withdrawal of our forces, two of our men were arrested. Let me say, I want to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You're getting ahead of me. I'm just asking about the moment -- the time when you returned to Prolom Banja, if at that time anyone who was in the group who returned was arrest or taken into custody because of the incident that happened at Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You indicate in your statement that you were told to go on leave. Were other members of the Skorpions also - who returned to Prolom Banja with you - also sent back home on leave?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You indicate in your statement that you were told once you returned to Prolom Banja to take some days off and to go back home on leave. Were other members of the Skorpions also allowed to take days off and just go on leave after returning to Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Podujevo incident, we remained for about ten days in Prolom Banja. We who didn't leave with the men who wanted to leave and go home immediately after the incident, expected to be sent to some other site. However, ten days after the incident, the SAJ commander came and told us to go on leave. His name was Zivko Trajkovic. He personally came, lined us up, and told us, "Now you're going back to Serbia. You're going home." We returned our weapons. However, we retained our uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You had told us that on the bus returning to Prolom Banja Dragan Medic had gotten up and said, "I did it." Was he questioned about this once he returned to Prolom Banja, about his possible participation in this incident?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially nobody was questioned, but I assume that the unit commander was his brother. I believe that the commander, i.e., his brother, definitely questioned him about the event in his hotel room. However, officially, nobody was taken into custody or arrested, nor was there any internal investigation carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 63 you speak about being contacted some days after when you had already returned to Sid, and you say that you returned to -- or were redeployed to Podujevo sometime around mid-April 1999. Earlier, you had read the names of the persons who were in the courtyard or that you saw in the courtyard. Were any of those persons returned to Podujevo with you when you returned -- to Kosovo when you were redeployed there in April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First let me correct you. We were not redeployed to Podujevo but, rather, to Kosovo Polje. Of the men that I had claimed have taken part in the execution of the civilians, only Cvetan Sasa didn't return. All the rest returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday and also today you were telling us that after the Kumanovo Agreement two persons were detain. Who were these persons who were arrested in connection with this incident at Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sasa Cvetan and Dejan Demirovic were arrested, and later on they were processed. Cvetan Sasa was sentenced to 20 years of prison, and Dejan Demirovic was acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you told us this arrest happened after the Kumanovo Agreement. So when exactly would that be in? Do you recall the month approximately when that -- when these arrests took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would that have been after the war had ended, the conflict in Kosovo, or was the conflict in Kosovo still going on? If you recall. If you don't recall, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict ended after the Serbian security forces withdrew from Kosovo and KFOR was -- was deployed there. Therefore, in that period there was no war in Kosovo any longer nor any NATO bombardment of Serbia. Everything had stopped, and that is -- that was the time when they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know for how long they were kept in detention, these two persons, once they were arrested? If you recall approximately.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you that I personally did not know these two men. I saw them for the first time in my life then in Podujevo. They were new men to the Skorpions. They had not been in the unit before. But when they got out of prison, when they were released from custody, I ran into them on the same day in Novi Sad, in a cafe, and they told me they had spent ten days in custody, and they told me they had not been arrested by the public security policemen but by the state security men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, yesterday just before we had our -- the end of the session, you indicated that Sasa Cvetan had been tried twice and that you testified as a witness, and you said that you had lied on one of these occasions. Can we first focus on the first trial again of Sasa Cvetan. How was it that you were called as a witness in that trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that trial was not publicised or covered by media reports so widely as nowadays. The trial was held in a small town. I believe it was called Prokuplje. And Sasa Cvetan was tried and Dejan Demirovic was tried in absentia because he had already emigrated to Canada. I was initially contacted by Defence counsel. I was in a law office of a Belgrade lawyer for some of my business, but when he found out who I was, he asked if I could appear as a witness for Sasa Cvetan. So it was at his insistence that I appeared as a witness. Because in our judicial system, the Defence and the Prosecution don't call witnesses; they just suggest witnesses to the Trial Chamber, and then the Trial Chamber decides who will appear as a witness. So he suggested me, and I told at the trial the story that the lawyer had prepared for me on an A4 paper, basically giving an alibi to Sasa Cvetan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did anyone else other than the lawyer speak to you about what you had to say during your testimony in this trial, in the first trial against Sasa Cvetan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when I set out for the courthouse, there were four of us witnesses in one car; and Commander Medic invited us to stop by his farm in Ruma, that's we are has a farm, and he told us -- he told me, "Any traitor will not live much longer." And apart from him, I was also approached by the family of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did any of the other persons who testified - you said you were four in total in the car - tell the truth about what happened at Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that trial in Prokuplje, the only person -- the only people who told the truth were two members of the active-duty SAJ and Commander Tutinac. All the rest of us told our story as we had been coached.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you feel about lying at those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was a very peculiar situation when several idiots kill small children. I could not find any justification in patriotic feelings or whatever, and at that moment I decided if I'm ever call as a witness again I'll tell the real story; but at that time I did not know the trial would be repeated. You have to understand my head was at stake. The consequences of telling the truth without any protection - and at that time in the judicial system of Serbia the institution of insider witness did not exist at all - would have been horrible, and I could not even contemplate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that there was a second trial against Sasa Cvetan, and you have said that today. Where did this second trial take place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second trial was held in Belgrade. There was a special chamber for war crimes in the District Court of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how was it that you were called as a witness in this second trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply the Trial Chamber re-invited all the witnesses that had appeared in the first trial plus some additional witnesses. So I was already on record as a witness in the first trial, and I was automatically summoned to the second one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you tell a different version of the incident at this second trial than what you had told the court in the first trial against Sasa Cvetan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not call it a different version. I would call it the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what made you change your mind about telling the truth this second time that you testified about this incident?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that trial in Belgrade, some of the children who survived the massacre testified before me, and I followed the media reports of their testimony, and I told all my acquaintances and friends among the Skorpions that if I am asked to appear as a witness by the court I will say that the crime had been committed by the Skorpions. That was the decision I had made. Secondly, I had no moral right -- you see, some NGOs in Serbia condemned the whole MUP and the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit for this crime, whereas I know that the regular SAJ and MUP have no involvement and no blame for this, and that's why I decided to tell the truth. Then after that, I was granted protective measures, special protective measures, by the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I with like to show two exhibits to the witness. These are 00951 and 00952.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you could first look at the larger -- the thicker document you have there. Do you recognise that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the top I see "Judge Biljana Sinanovic." I remember her. She was the Presiding Judge at the trial in Belgrade; and this must be the verdict, the judgement in the trial against Sasa Cvetan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you now look at the second document, the thinner document, and tell me if you recognise that document.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the confirmed judgement, the confirmed trial judgement, confirmed by the Supreme Court. This is a verdict of the Supreme Court confirming the trial judgement. You must know that I am not a professional lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender these two exhibits these are 00951 and 00952, and I ask that those two exhibits be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received. Already they are exhibits. 951 is Exhibit P40, 952 is Exhibit P41.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sorry. I was not aware of that, Your Honours. At this stage I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djurdjic, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a couple of questions. Could I just see P40 again? It slipped by me somehow. Could we call it up again on the screen, because I think the witness has seen the judgement, but he did not look at the date. We did not see the date, so I'm not quite sure which judgement it was. 17 June 2005. And could we now call up P41. Yes. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my name is Veljko Djurdjic, I'm a member of the Defence team of the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. I'm being assisted by Ms. Mary O'Leary, member of the team, whereas the lead counsel Dragoljub Djordjevic is temporarily absent. You have more experience before this Tribunal than I do, so I will just remind you to speak more slowly as we speak the same language so that the interpreters and the court reporter can do their job properly and that all that we say is properly recorded. Mr. Stoparic, would I be right in saying that, guided by patriotic reasons, you joined the volunteers in 1999?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no other reasons I could have had apart from patriotism.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that your only motivation in 1999 was your desire to join in at the request of Slobodan Medic to defend the country against the NATO aggression and against the activities of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you had never committed any crime against the civilian population in all your years of warfare -- of soldiering?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortunately I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From 1991 until end 1999, all your activities were strictly within the framework of the military operations your participated in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or let's make it even more specific. Sometimes I just held my position as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that as a commander of the Scouts Platoon in 1999 you did not issue an order to your subordinates to kill Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. The only order that I could have given them was to kill any terrorist they run into.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right in saying that as the commander of the Scouts Platoon you never issued an order to your subordinates to expel Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Apart from this unfortunate incident in Podujevo, I never even had any contact with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right in saying that as the commander of the Scouts Platoon you never issued an order to your subordinates to torch Albanian houses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the moment when I was wounded, which I believe was on the 2nd of May, I never even entered densely populated areas. We only passed through several empty Mahalas. I didn't even hear of any houses that were burnt. We did some clearing of forests, and we rarely came across any populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My question was: Is it true that you never gave any orders to your subordinates to torch Albanian houses in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a high-ranking officer, but I was the commander of the Scouts Platoon, which would be the strike-force of my unit; and our only activity is military action. After we perform our action, other units take over while we rest. So the very idea that some of my soldiers could have torched anything on their own initiative is impossible. I never issued an order of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you as the commander of the Scouts Platoon during the 1999 war never issued an order to your subordinates to destroy mosques or other religious buildings in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just make it clear. You are saying no to "Am I right," or "Did you issue an order?"

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never issued an order for a religious or cultural structure to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that during the 1999 war you as the commander of the Scouts Platoon were never ordered to kill Albanian civilians by anyone? You were never ordered to expel them, to set their houses on fire, to take away their IDs and other documents and shred them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received such orders from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly as saying that you were proud that as a reservist of the MUP you would be attached to the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very proud you could say. May I add one thing? I considered that as a reward for all my prior experience. I thought that the security background checks had been run and somebody up there knew that I had always made every effort to behave appropriately. I did not need to know about Geneva Conventions, but in a war if you asked me whether a woman holding a baby in her arms should be shot or not, I wouldn't need a Geneva Convention to tell me that it's wrong. There is something inside me that would have been against it, that would not have allowed me to do it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stoparic, am I right in saying that in peacetime the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, SAJ of the MUP of Serbia, does not have a reserve force?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said as much to the Prosecutor when she questioned me. This was an extraordinary situation. As far as I know, they perform extraordinary tasks in peacetime, and they did not need a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that on the 23rd of March, 1999, a state of immediate threat of war had been declared?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I know the system. There was first a declaration of the immediate threat of war and then a declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you set out to Kosovo and Metohija when the NATO aggression against Serbia, that is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, had already started?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was already two or three days into the NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a general mobilisation had been declared?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that once the general mobilisation had been declared, all conscripts were called up to report according to their wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to their military evidentiary speciality and their wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that Mr. Slobodan Medic, when he came to Sid, told you that you would be assigned to the reserve force of the MUP and that you would be assigned to the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember clearly when I asked if I would be in the army or the police. He said I would be in the police. He didn't say I would be in the reserve force of the police. He said we would be in coordinated action with the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stoparic, would I be right in saying that any and all persons who set out towards Kosovo and Metohija as members of the reserve force of the MUP had previously done their regular military service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the regulations, they should have. But I believe that in that group of our volunteers, there were one or two people who had slipped by without meeting that requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Because you yourself had done your regular military service. Am I right in saying that every recruit, when they report for their regular military service, is familiarised with the rules of warfare and the Geneva Conventions during their basic training?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that when I served in the reconnaissance infantry during my regular military service, I was trained by the -- in the rules and customs of war as part of my training. I did my military service in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since you have experience, military experience in both peacetime and in wartime, can you tell me that the basic training is common to all regardless of the their speciality, is common to all recruits?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First there is general basic training, boot camp and other drills before you are sent to specialised training. And as part of the basic trainings, you are trained in all the rules and customs of war, and there is within the framework of that both practical and theoretical training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that after your first meeting with Mr. Slobodan Medic in March 1999 in Sid, you drew up a list of individuals who wanted to go to Kosovo and Metohija and that the same list was held by Petar Petrasevic, if I understood you correctly, and another colleague of yours was also given a notebook with a list of names of people who were to engage. Can you clarify this for me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Pero Petrasevic was given an official task by Medic to make lists of people who wanted to go. It took 24 hours to draw up these lists. People know me in Sid, and people knew that I was headed for the theatre of war. Once the people learned about the fact that people were to be sent to Kosovo, people came to me because they knew that I was in the game. After that, the lists that I made, I gave them to Pero Petrasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind the entire group of men who were headed towards Kosovo, from your former unit of the oil industry of Krajina only a very few people, and that were the main people, headed towards Kosovo and Metohija together with you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The leadership and some that I also used to make up my unit. They were experienced men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that you said, and correct me if I'm wrong, that your Reconnaissance Platoon numbered 30 men.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you exactly. The Reconnaissance Platoon was divided into two squads. One was headed by me. The other was headed by Milovan Tomic. These two squads numbered up to 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So these were quite sizable squad, 15 men each.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Reconnaissance Squads have a different task than normal and ordinary squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, when you look at the leading structure in your unit, and I'm referring to company, platoon, commanders, and other commanding officer, how many other men had been with you in the unit that protected the oil refineries?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of them were already in command of platoons. The majority of those who were not with Skorpion were known to have been in other units. It was not a requirement for them to be with the Skorpions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this second tier structure that we talked about, how many men were there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Kosovo with approximately 120 men, excluding the commander and his deputy as commanding officer. They were divided into four platoons and one Reconnaissance Platoon. Each platoon was made up of two or more squads. So, one platoon had a platoon commander and several squad commanders. So the commanding structure would be 4 times 3, plus we in the Reconnaissance Platoon, and the commander, and his deputy; and also to be added to that that should be the commander of the active forces who was entitled to issue orders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stoparic. You have just answered my question concerning the men who left as a unit. Just to add up the figures, you said 14 -- actually, 12 plus 2 is 14, plus the commander and the deputy makes the total of 16. So this was the command structure.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plus/minus one man because one platoon could have had more squads than the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that among these men were volunteers who were born and were living in the territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there were men in our unit born in Serbia, yes. I was born in Serbia. But in our unit deployed in Kosovo were people who had been living in Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, just to make it clearer for you. The majority of the unit members were men who -- who later became refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stoparic, am I right to say that -- I'm referring to the unit commanded by Slobodan Medic and the meetings held at that level. You didn't attend any other meetings at any higher command level?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever these meetings took place he would attend if invited. According to my rank and according to the rules of service, I couldn't attend a meeting where you had colonels in presence. I was a squad or platoon commander. Only if he had some specific task to be carried out on the ground, that's a different story; but according to my job description, so to speak, I couldn't have attended such meetings, but the commander did though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right to say that all the knowledge you have about what transpired at the higher command meetings came from Mr. Slobodan Medic who conveyed to you what happened in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would sometimes escort him to the building where the meetings was taking place, but I couldn't attend any briefings. He himself would only convey the orders that he thought were appropriate on a need-to-know basis to be conveyed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Slobodan Medic like to brag?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're the first one to ask me that. He was an egotist. He liked to brag about things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on this for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and all of us if possible?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Medic for years. You use the word "to brag." Yes, he liked to exaggerate his role in the war . I don't know how to describe this. If I use some bad words, people will say that I hate him. Therefore, I'm reluctant to use some bad language.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to insist on this any longer. I understand your point. I wanted to ask you this: Are you aware that he was the commander of the Territorial Defence in the village of Banovci in 1991 when the independent autonomous district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was established?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Whether he was the commander for a period of time and then replaced by someone else, but anyway, he was in the Territorial Defence of the Vinkovacki Banovci village, his native village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in his capacity of the commander of the TO, Vinkovacki Banovci, he was appointed commander of a group that was a signed to guard the oil fields of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially I know that Mrgud appointed him to this post taking into account the reputation that he enjoyed in the area and that with his TEO and with the assistance of the Yugoslav People's Army, he liberated this area and of course taking into consideration his good knowledge of the area and the terrain. I know that he was appointed to this post, that is, to guard a vitally important infrastructural facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that these oil fields at the time in 1991 were on the separation line with the Republic of Croatia? Let's say that there's -- the border was close to these fields or in the fields themselves.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Luckily there was a natural border and that was the River Bosut. That is where the frontier was. Therefore, guarding the oil drills, we had our zone of responsibility stretching along the River Bosut in the length of 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that after the Croatian army had attacked the Medak Pocket, in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, on the principle of double criteria, units from that territory took weapons and artillery and that the command of the army of the republic -- of Serbian Krajina was established?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. One part of the Knin Karija [phoen] and part of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem were declared a single state without any territorial connections and with a single army and with a single command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right to say that in the aftermath of this event, this security detail was placed under the command of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, i.e., became part of it as a specially trained and best-equipped independent unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember General Loncar, who was supposed to be the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it fair to say that after the signing of the Erdut Agreement sometime in mid-1996, I don't know of the exact date, the oil fields were handed over to the United Nations? First answer me this.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Djelatovac we managed to build a barracks and this was also handed over to the blue helmets. These were dark-skinned lads. I don't know from which country they came, including the oil fields. As for the weapons, we drove it to the Sid with the escort of the Serbian police and handed it over to the barracks -- at the barracks, including all the armoured equipment and all the infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it fair to say that the unit that was guarding the Krajina oil fields was disbanded and ceased to exist in mid 1996?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, immediately after the Erdut Agreement this took place. And that did not exist in any of the Serbian military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that many the unit of the oil industry of Krajina had never been a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm someone who does not believe in paramilitary formations, and there was no way for us to be paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let us summarise. Up until 1993, this was the unit securing the oil facilities of Krajina, and after the mobilisation, it was placed under the command of the corps of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and then in 1996, following the hand-over of the oil fields, this unit was disbanded and ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the conclusion that we have reached. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stoparic, am I right to say that you left Novi Sad in buses, which is mentioned in your statement, and that you reached the area of Bubanj Potok where you stopped in order to be issued uniforms and weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just remembered, and I didn't mention that in my statement. When we were mobilised an order was that none of us should take any of our old uniforms so that we wouldn't look like a motley crew and that they would all -- that we would all be issued identical uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that you, as MUP reservists, were issued uniforms with the camouflage garment in the field where you stopped?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received the whole kit, uniforms, boots, et cetera, except for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that on the caps that you were issued, there was an emblem of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia with the tricolour of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the emblem in force at the time. It has a yellow strip and a flag in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that the officials of the MUP who were distributing the uniforms did not give you any emblems of the Skorpion, that is the unit that used to exist in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to the Prosecutor's question, I said that Srdjan Manojlovic was the one who distributed the Skorpion's emblems. Some of them even had SAJ emblems which I understand only that they obtained it by themselves. The officials distributing this to -- to us didn't give us any other emblems other than those that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned weapons, so let us wrap up this topic. Am I right to say that you were issued weapons only once you arrived at the accommodation centre in Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons was following us either from Belgrade or I don't know from where. It was loaded on a truck, but you have to understand that due to the bombing, we were travelling in a stretched column in order to deceive NATO that this was an army formation. I don't know exactly when we were joined by this truck-load of weapons, and we were given weapons in Prolom Banja. It was an entirely new load of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right to say that you were accommodated in Prolom Banja in a hotel that was used for accommodation by the MUP of the Republic of Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who owned this hotel, whether it was MUP or not, but we stayed there. I didn't like that idea. I was afraid of the bombing. I would have preferred to stayed -- to have stayed in tents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us locate precisely Prolom Banja now. If I can be of assistance. Is it correct that Prolom Banja is located in the so-called Serbia proper, that is, before the administrative boundary with the province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prolom Banja is in Serbia proper before Djavulja Varos, because Djavulja Varos is the first settlement across the border of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now that you mentioned Djavulja Varos, can I conclude that you used the old road to go from Prolom Banja to Podujevo? You did not use the main road?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Djavulja Varos because in anticipation of going out into the field to be deployed, I went there on my own, because it's a famous historical location where the Tzar Lazar gave communion to the troops before the battle of Kosovo in 1389. But now when you mention it, I don't know which road we used exactly to go to Podujevo, but it was somewhere in the vicinity of Djavulja Varos that we first got the news that we would be sent to Podujevo. That was the first I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that on the 28th of March you left Prolom Banja and went to Podujevo by buses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but we did go to Podujevo on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that upon arrival at Podujevo, after stepping off the bus, you received orders from commander Slobodan Medic to look for accommodation in abandoned local houses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first 15, 20 minutes we were not allowed to get off the bus. After that, the order was given that in that street, whose name I didn't know, we should find a place to stay because there would be no action for that day. We would spend the night there. And then the next day, we didn't know what was going to happen, but we expected some action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that at the moment when you got off the bus and you started looking for a place to stay, you were not yet placed at the -- under the command of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Nobody told me that I was under the command of such and such a person. I knew that Medic could not be the Commander-In-Chief. That was perfectly clear. But nobody told me that we would be under their command three hours later. Whether we were already under their command or not, whether it was already decided at that time or it was decided later, I wouldn't be able to say; because as we were looking for a place to stay, there were also SAJ policemen around, PJP policemen around, other troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not quite precise in my question. You, at the moment when you were stepping off the bus and starting to look for a place to stay, you had not yet been placed under any particular command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not aware of it, although it would have been stupid if it had been that way. It would have been like we were on a school trip to Kosovo. Somebody must have decided something about our place in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, those are two different things, the actual state of affairs, and what had been decided in theory. They didn't always coincide. But never mind. Am I right in saying that at the moment of your arrival the department of internal affairs in Podujevo had been damaged by NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost sure that I had seen that building damaged, and that was not strange. Police stations were the first target for NATO airplanes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Precisely because of that well-known fact, am I right in saying that all the buildings of military use such as military barracks and police stations were relocated at the beginning of the aggression?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our officers did not go to school for nothing. All the buildings, all the departments that were supposed to be targeted by NATO were relocated, and all the efforts were made to camouflage whatever could not be relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the place where you stopped, where your buses stopped in Podujevo, was at least one kilometre away from the building that used to house the Department of Internal Affairs in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say now. It was not across the street from the bus, certainly, but whether it was one kilometre away or less, I couldn't tell exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I understand. It was quite a few years ago. Am I right in saying that when you got off the bus Mr. Slobodan Medic went to attend a meeting at the command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I answer? Yes. Mr. Slobodan Medic left to attend a meeting with someone, we didn't know who. And you're right, at that moment, all our troops were under the command of platoon commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not accompany Mr. Medic to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the members of our unit did accompany him, but not me. I never even said I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I add? I don't think this meeting was being held indoors, because of the NATO air-strikes. I think they were holding it in some sort of yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to come back to those documents, the judgement and the appeal that we have seen before. Is it the case that the trial first began against Cvetan and Demirovic in the District Court in Prokuplje.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if it's the District Court or not, but it's in Prokuplje. And I believe that's actually the Pristina court that was relocated to Prokuplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that it is the District Court that handles homicide. But that court was later moved to Belgrade, and Judge Sinanovic took over the case. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And Judge Sinanovic issued the judgement in that case for the first time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She determined the maximum sentence envisaged by our law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, 20 years is the maximum sentence. But that was the traditional District Court, and the Appeals Court varied, annulled that sentence, that judgement.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was abroad at the time. Possibly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But look at the dates. We saw that the judgement was from 2005. Do you still have it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28th June, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So this judgement and the decision of the Appeals Court to reject the appeal resulted in the final judgement in this case but only when the trial was renewed, when the case was retried.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, but I didn't know that the Supreme Court had ordered a retrial, but I can see it now from the dates, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right that after that judgement, proceedings were initiated against another four persons for the same crime in Podujevo of the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There had been investigation, and this case is now in the phase of trial against these four other people, and the case is known as Podujevo 2; and there is another insider witness involved, a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me about these four persons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Djukic is one of the accused. The second, Dragan Medic, Dragan Borojevic, and number four, Miodrag Solaja, and there is one protected witness involved. I know who the protected witness is, but I will not name him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said that one of the accused was Zeljko Djukic. Is that the one whose nickname was Brka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The man who on your way back from Podujevo said that he himself had three children and which idiot had committed this crime?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I get it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will have the first break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, what I would like you now to tell me is something about what Mrs. Kravetz asked you about concerning the investigation that you conducted at the time when you left Podujevo and went to Prolom Banja. How did you carry out this internal investigation, and did it yield any results?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain you in this way: The majority of men, who did not take part in the execution of these innocent civilians, of course disagreed with the whole thing. We carried out an unofficial internal investigation. Various commanders of squads tried to find, including myself, whether anyone from my platoon took part in any of that. I might have missed something. But my impression is that this investigation was obstructed by the commander. This is just my supposition, and it is based on the reason that the commander's brother took part in that. Therefore, it was possible that our investigation revealed who those involved were, but that is where it stopped. Nothing else happened. Maybe I and other people as well should have gone to the first next police station and reported once we got home. I didn't think, though, that it was necessary. I thought that the police would do their job as they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So you did internally what you did, but nothing that was discovered was passed on either to the commander, who you said obstructed it, nor to any of the organs that were supposed to be engaged in this.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I know that you were seriously wounded in May, but I would like to ask you something else. Do you believe me when I tell you that the Podujevo organ of the internal affairs submitted on the -- filed, on the 23rd of May, criminal reports against Sasa Cvetan and Dejan Demirovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing for me to believe. I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you also know that on the same date the district public prosecutor's office in Prokuplje filed a request to the court in Prokuplje to investigate Sasa Cvetan and Demirovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victims' bodies were still on the crime screen. The crime screen was secured, and the investigating judge arrived on the spot, including the police organs. They carried out an on-site investigation, retrieved the cartridges, but I didn't see it myself because I was sent back to Prolom Banja, but I knew that that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, 1999, the District Court in Prokuplje issued a decision to investigate Sasa Cvetan and Dejan Demirovic. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but it sounds logical. I said that Sasa Cvetan and Dejan Demirovic were arrested after the Kumanovo Agreement and it makes sense that, according to this, an investigation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let he is now go back to the Kumanovo Agreement. Do you know when the Kumanovo Agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in hospital at the time. I see the Kumanovo Agreement as the point when the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said that it was in June 1999 that the Kumanovo Agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I know that these two were arrested after our forces left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that you are mistaken? A short while ago during your testimony you said that when you left hospital that you met these two in a cafe in some town.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novi Sad, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But towards the end of June or in early July was the time when you left hospital. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent two or three days first in Pristina hospital then at the Batanjica in Belgrade; and I was attached a device in Belgrade, and I left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I'm asking you these questions because I have a decision to carry out investigation issued by the Prokuplje District Court, dated 24th May, 1999, in which it is stated that Sasa Cvetan and Demirovic Dejan were to be placed in detention counting as of 21st of May, 1999, which would only indicate that they were arrested at the time, but that when you met them a month later, it seems that they were released from detention.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They may have been placed in detention on the date that you mentioned, but the question is whether they managed to arrest them all. I don't know. I would have no objection if they had spent three months in detention. But I think that they told me that they spent ten days, and believe me, I have no reason to add anything to my statement that is not true. I may have got the dates mixed up, but this is what I know about this as being the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that following the filing of a criminal report, the MUP organs or the police have no further influence on the duration and the procedure of the processes conducted by courts?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only based on an additional prosecutor's orders they can extend investigation to involve other persons. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Everything that we talked about so far concerning the duration of trial is in the hands of the court and judiciary. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it fair to say -- actually, I am right, because a minute ago you said that ten days after your return to Podujevo, Zivko Trajkovic came and told you that you would be going home. Now, did you return your weapon in Prolom Banja or did you do that something on your way from Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. We were sent to a facility in Belgrade, and believe me, as I sit here today I cannot tell you whether I put my rifle on a truck in Prolom Banja or if I did that in this facility in Belgrade or in the suburbs of Belgrade. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then conclude that if one-third of members of your unit immediately on the 28th left Prolom Banja, that some 70 or 80 of you went home from Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I should say so. The first men who went away returned their weapons in Prolom Banja and left, and by simple arithmetic that would be the number of the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that after a certain period of time following your return to Sid, you were contacted by Pero Petrasevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you also contacted by Zeljko Djukic, aka Brka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you know that? I think that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this is written in your statements. You mentioned the nickname, and then you mentioned the name today.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I have forgotten what I said in my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That was the Brka who got cross when he was on the bus and who is currently on trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was discussed on that occasion between Petrasevic, Brka, and yourself?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that they -- we were going back to Kosovo. I could have remembered better this conversation earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, whatever you cannot remember, just say that you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is something important, please remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will move on. Let us move on. I'm sorry you don't remember. Am I right to say that for the second time you went and were billeted in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that apart from your unit in Kosovo Polje, there was no other unit with the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that there was another unit as well, but I cannot say for sure that they were attached to the SAJ. Why do I think that? Because I saw soldiers who used to fight in Bosnia and -- as volunteers, and they were definitely on the police reserve, but I cannot say whether they participated in coordinated actions with PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you took part in the action Malo Jezerce as a member of the MUP reserve attached to the SAJ. In addition to active personnel of the SAJ and your unit, no one else took part in this operation; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that in Malo Jezerce operation was not then operation in which the VJ took part nor the unit for special operations or JSO?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say -- see any members of the JSO or the Yugoslav Army, because in the actions that we carried out together with the SAJ, we didn't need any support in terms of heavy artillery. We had one or two mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what your task was in the Jezerce operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task was to clear the terrain from the pockets of resistance by the KLA, to clear the elevations. I remember even one elevation that held a repeater, and that was an important feature for us. To drive them out and to liquidate them, if necessary, in action and to get control of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you performed this task as set out in a disciplined manner?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking for me personally, yes, because I received a commendation from professionals such as Tutinac and Trajkovic. I even got a decoration on the 13th of May, the day of security. I always tried as hard as I could be professional in my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That decoration that you received from the Minister Vlatko Stojiljkovic, was it also a declaration for the entire unit that participated in the action?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was meant to include the whole unit. It was in my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean this literally.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well if you allow me to add. In that second deployment in Kosovo, in that second field mission, not only I but the majority of us made every effort to demonstrate to the SAJ officers that what happened in Kosovo does not qualify all of us that we can be disciplined and that we can act in accordance with all the rules and customs of war, and I believe we were successful. And until I was wounded, I believe we did an excellent job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that during this operation in which you were involved until you were wounded, that Albanian civilians, whom you had seen from afar, were withdrawing with their belongings together with the KLA as the KLA was pulling out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my second field mission I saw groups of Albanian civilians several times, and infiltrated among them members of the KLA. I would see them at the distance of 1 or 2 kilometres, and they were retreating somewhere. But let me say that I was wounded by a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mean a member of the KLA dressed as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But technically speaking, you as a reconnaissance squad were searching the terrain while the remainder of the unit was sealing off the area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We as the Reconnaissance Platoon were supposed to mop up the terrain and clear the pockets of resistance. It was a choice between eliminating them or running them -- into them again. The first night the remainder of the unit succeeded in keeping control of the terrain while we got time to rest before we continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that the remainder of the unit, that is the part of the unit that was not the Reconnaissance Platoon, was stationary, and their job was to maintain control of the terrain that you had already cleared?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that every unit is divided into platoons, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd, and it's not by accident that the 1st Platoon is called the 1st Platoon. It is composed of the best troops, and the other platoons are supposed to support the 1st Platoon. So the 1st Platoon would sometimes take part in the action if we needed it, and the other platoons were engaged in the job that you just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in this second field mission in April and May 1999, you were not present at a single meeting, save for meetings within your unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, in that field mission we would reach a point, let's say a forest, and Tutinac would be in the forest. If he would hold a small meeting like a briefing, I would attend; but I would never go to a special meeting where I would be invited to come as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not mean briefings that were held as part of the action but outside the action.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I would get orders from Tutinac himself because Tutinac monitored the action, and he would assign me wherever he thought I would be the most useful because he is a great professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But outside of the action, you never attended any meetings outside of your unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my second field mission I was practically in action all the time until I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: After you were wounded, you said you were immediately transferred to hospital in Pristina where you had surgery, and then you were transferred to the orthopaedic clinic in the neighbourhood of Batajnica, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now could you explain greater detail what was your status? What were your rights as a wounded member of the reserve force of the MUP? How long did it last? What kind of material support did you receive, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's go back a few years. It was not the first time I was wounded. I had been wounded earlier before, and I was not able to exercise any of my entitlements because I did not have the necessary documentation. Facing a medical panel once, a man on the panel told me that as far as he is concerned, I was wounded in a settlement of accounts between different Mafia gangs, if I don't have the papers to show that it happened during the war. The first step in the army would be to see the doctor in the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, Dr. Dragan Markovic, who had helped those unfortunate children; and he monitored my progress when I was at home or in hospital. In all that time I would go to the base of the SAJ to pick up my salary. I went every two months to appear before a medical panel so that they would extend my sick leave for another two months. Everything was done professionally and according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned the SAJ base. I want to follow up on that. Am I right in saying that from the moment the war started until you were discharged from the hospital in June or July 1999, you did not visit the SAJ base in Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only see passing by in my car those special vehicles, and I would, on the basis of that, know that it was the SAJ base, but I never went inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So only when you were discharged from the hospital did you go to the SAJ base for the first time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that I visited many times. I was received. I had lunch with members of the SAJ, and I received my salary there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But that was all after the war, after the war ended?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, is it correct -- we've finished with that part where you served of in the army, but is it correct that in 1999, when you first went out into the field as a volunteer, you spent seven days in the TO of Slavonia -- Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and that after those seven days you got a call-up from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first engagement in the war was as part of the Territorial Defence of Baranja, Slavonia, and Western Srem, which was also under the JNA command because we were one state. The Territorial Defence of that area was also under the command of the JNA. And then I was attached to the 1st Guards Brigade, and I was sent to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong. You got a call-up from the JNA to report to the 1st Guards Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were already out in the field. My whole platoon was reassigned. We did get a call-up, but we were not supposed to go to Belgrade. They had already arrived where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But was it an oral call-up or a written call-up?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we reported to that captain, he gave us certificates that we had reported. So you can call it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's what I mean. Were you mobilised practically when you went to the 1st Guards Brigade because you had received your wartime assignment there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in -- my rights and obligations did not change from when I was a volunteer to when I became a reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about the various assignments in that brigade, but in 1991 you were in Djelatovac as a member of the JNA, and that's where you met -- when you met --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did you -- when were you demobed from the JNA, which year?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vukovar, I was assigned to the Leva Supoderica unit. And Leva Supoderica unit was subordinated to the 1st Guards Brigade. So you can reckon that I was a reservist of the JNA until Vukovar fell, officially speaking. And for the field service in Vukovar, I received my salary when I went to Topcider in Belgrade to the base of the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In lines 20, 21, and 22 there was a name that put in your question that the interpreter missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think I remember. Let's clear it up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it right, Mr. Stoparic, I said that as a conscript in 1991 you were in Djelatovac and that's when you met Mr. Slobodan Medic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then I continued with my other questions. Just tell me what year did Vukovar fall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar fell in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And after Vukovar did you leave the Army of Yugoslavia and go to Sid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Vukovar fell the Guards Brigade retreated from the Vukovar area following orders. Another brigade came to replace it, and I, like the others, went on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you demobed? Were you demobed and go to Sid? You returned your military equipment and went to Sid.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From my statement -- from your statement I understood that in 1993, upon the invitation of Slobodan Medic, you left Sid to join a unit that provided security services to the oil industry of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993. And I think that because I was rehabilitating at home from my first injury sustained in the vicinity of Mostar. That's where he found me and suggested that I join his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.
