Am I right in saying that at that time, when you joined the unit that guarded the oil industry of Krajina, the petroleum industry of Krajina, 30 per cent of that unit had wartime experience, 30 per cent were Red Berets earlier, and 30 per cent were locals from Djelatovac who had no experience?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't say that 30 per cent were former Red Berets. There were 30 per cent of members in the Skorpions who had gone through some kind of training. Training went on in Bajzos [phoen] and another location which was the base of that notorious unit of the Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. That's what I meant when I said 30 per cent. There were 30 per cent of men who had some sort of specialised training. When the war began, all we had was the regular military service we had done in the Yugoslav People's Army, but the war demonstrated that that was not enough, that additional training was needed so that we could do our job properly. Thirty per cent had no wartime experience. They just sat around in Djelatovac. They did know how to handle weapons, but they had no training that would allow them to participate in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But is it correct that part of the unit always stayed on oil fields and guarded them at all times?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we received orders for a field mission, we the Skorpions had two companies. One company plus the Scouts Platoon would go out into the field, and one company would stay. The next field mission, the company that had earlier stayed on base would now go into the field and the other company would stay on the oil fields, but the Reconnaissance Platoon would always go into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when exactly did you leave that unit that guarded the petroleum industry of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to remember exactly. As soon as I joined the unit, I was assigned to the Reconnaissance Platoon, and later I received orders to conduct training for the Reconnaissance Platoon. That was my first duty with the Skorpions. But when the Skorpions went on field missions sometimes, I went with them as a volunteer. I did not go as a member of the Skorpions, because every time when we would go into the field, the commander would raise me and say, "You are coming with us."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think at one point, perhaps yesterday, you said that after Velika Kladusa and the poisoning suffered by members of your unit, you left the unit. When was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's good that you reminded me of this. You're right. After the mission in Velika Kladusa where we were poisoned, the majority of people contracted either diphtheria or hepatitis and we were placed in quarantine. That is when I left the unit. Not because of that incident, but because I simply decided that it was enough. As for the time-line, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I cannot find this particular paragraph in your statements, but concerning your transfer from Slavonia and Baranja when one travels to Bosnia and the embargo imposed on it; is it right to say that in 1993 this was subject to a special procedure, and this border was not as porous as it was described?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a special procedure. We secretly went across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you made some corrections in your 2006 statement regarding your engagement in JSO unit for special operations. Can you tell us briefly what your engagement involved and what the training was about and how it all ended?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the so-called Croatian Operation Storm was either under way or was imminent. I was in my hometown, and I received information from a state security operative. He hailed from Sremska Mitrovica, and I suppose that he was a state security operative. I used to meet him on several occasions before when he asked me for some information. He asked me, "What are you doing? You see, the problems are going to rise in the front, and are you planning to go?" I said, "Maybe." He said, "If you want to go, here's telephone number. Go to the Omorica Hotel, ask the front desk to dial this number for you, and join these guys there and join them in their actions." And that is what I did. I went to the Omorica Hotel on Mount Tara, dialed the number. A policeman in Lada Niva car arrived, and he took me to the Hotel Tara where we were told to wait for a sufficient number of candidates to assemble. It took some time then an officer came, I don't remember who he was; it was breakfast-time, and he asked me and told me, "Since we are waiting for the instructors to come and since I see from your CV that you are a reserve officer, why don't you conduct some limited training until we all gather together." So while the people were being assembled, I conducted the training that I was capable of doing. Of course, I didn't train any of the active-duty personnel. This was officially dubbed at the time the JSO Reserve Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did you return to Sid and cease to be a member of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Erdut Agreement I don't know the date but that could be taken as a bench-mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, let me just go back to something that I saw in your statement, but I think that we have more or less covered everything in this section. Can you explain to me something in paragraph 49 which I cannot understand. You said younger members of the local MUP stations in Serbia were assigned to the Special Unit of Police in Kosovo, but they carried out their task as part of the Special Pol Units [as interpreted] under the direction of MUP. Can you explain this to me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was probably my answer to somebody's question. What was the difference between the JSO, SAJ, and PJP. I have limited knowledge about this because you yourself know that I was not an active-duty policeman. What I tried to say was that members of the PJP came from all the OUP in the Republic of Serbia that is to say, younger and more able-bodied policemen who in peacetime carried out there normal duties in their respective police stations; however, in some intervention of circumstances, they were considered to be PJP. I don't know if my definition was correct, but that was my assumption. I think it's fair. And I tried to explain what the difference between the PJP because those who asked me this question didn't know the difference or what the PJP meant. They thought it was a regular police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that the PJP units were engaged, if the requirements were fulfilled, in some other places in Serbia outside of Kosovo and Metohija as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were engaged in all extraordinary situations or emergency situations that involved, for example, the arrest of local criminals, big-shot criminals. So as I said in any kind of emergency situation, if the chief of the commander of this unit would decide so, they were deployed. Because you would agree with me that in those years we had a huge number of refugees, a lot of illegal weapons, and the PJP was justified in existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But let me just reiterate once again I cannot say with absolute certainty that this is how the PJP was structured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I saw somewhere in your statement that you mentioned that a platoon commander was someone called Milojevic Kinez.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predrag Milojevic aka Kinez.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where is he now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has been convicted for the crimes in Ovcara in 1991, and he received maximum punishment. I mentioned him as a platoon commander with the Skorpion for a period of time while we were in Kosovo. Namely Milojevic aka Kinez and a group of people from Ruma came to Prolom Banja and joined us after the incident. Later on, he went to another field mission. Milojevic Kinez was deemed to be a very experienced man among other volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Stoparic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have finished with my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you were asked by learned counsel for the Defence about your first deployment to Kosovo from Sid to Prolom Banja and then to Kosovo. When your unit the Skorpions unit was first deployed to Kosovo, were you kept together as a group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it's a matter of translation of the way you put your question, but I didn't understand your question. What do you mean kept together as a group? I don't understand. The Skorpion unit was a compact one and it remained as a group, if that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was referring to. Now, in your second you were asked question about your second deployment to Kosovo in April of 1999. When you -- your unit was deployed for a second time to Kosovo, were you again kept together as one unit or were individuals dispersed into separate detachments of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We were again a compact unit, and we were not seconded to other MUP units. We were constantly under the scrutiny of the SAJ, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You were asked questions about your return from Podujevo to Prolom Banja and specifically about Trajkovic visit to Prolom Banja some ten days after you had returned. When Trajkovic visited you at Prolom Banja, was he informed about the reasons why you had been sent back from Podujevo to Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only make an assumption. I have no information that he had any information, but it makes sense that he knew about the incident and that for that reason, though, he was sending us away from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about a visit that you had when you returned to Sid by a man by the name of Brka and Petrasevic, excuse me pronunciation, and you said that you were told that you were returning to Kosovo. This is before your second deployment. Can you tell us a bit of how the second deployment was organised?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us already had uniforms from our first mission. We didn't return our uniforms. We did so after the second field mission. It was organised in the same manner, only we didn't go first to Novi Sad, but, rather, we travelled by buses and we ended up in Pristina but without weapons. We also had with us our civilian clothes in order to try and deceive our enemies. I'm talking about NATO in this instance, because we thought that if we were wearing civilian clothes they would not attack our buses, whereas if we were in uniforms, they would definitely strike us. This is the detail that I remember now, and I don't think I mentioned it in my statement, that we travelled to Pristina in civilian clothes and that we put on our uniforms there that we already had with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When this Skorpions Unit was put together for the second time prior to your second deployment to Kosovo, was there any screening done as to who would be a member of this unit before being deployed to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For those who registered with me, I conducted my own screening. As for the others, I don't know. But I myself made the selection. For instance, a man comes to me, wants to go to the front, and I would just tell them there are no vacancies. Everything is filled. Because I knew all the locals from my town and from the general area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some questions about the ordering of torching of Albanian homes and whether you had issued any orders to torch Albanian homes, and you said that -- you were explaining how you carried out actions, and you said that after your unit perform your actions other units took over while you rested. Now, in your statement at paragraph 68, you described the practice of torching of houses or setting fire to houses and facilities by PJP units. When you were engaged during the second deployment to Kosovo, did other units who were engaged in actions with you carry out any torching of houses in the areas where you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Defence counsel asked me whether I had ordered anyone to take part in the torching of the houses, and I said no. Of course, I saw many houses that were already burnt down or were aflame. Some of them were probably intentionally set on fire, some were burned by NATO strikes; but the burning of houses is not something that is not common in war. That would be my answer. There were instances of houses being set on fire in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your statement you say that when you -- your unit took over a hamlet and you withdrew, and then a PJP unit would -- that were in the rear guard would set fire to all houses and facilities, destroying them, would this be the practice that was commonly employed while you were carrying out actions, that your unit would withdraw and then a PJP unit would come in and set fire to the area that was controlled or taken over?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't always the case it was a PJP. It might have been the army. I'm sure that on many occasions I regretted that everything was on fire and that I had to spend the night in the place that had been burned down. It would have been much better if the houses were intact. Houses were set on fire. That was a fact. I don't know who issued these orders, but you had fools and idiots in all units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was the purpose of setting the houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure -- let's take an example of a Mahala. Once the Albanians left and we'd take control of the terrain, they would come back from the forest after two days. I presume if you set somebody's house on fire that they have no place to go to or to go back to. I think that's the only reasonable conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stoparic, you'll be pleased to know that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your coming to The Hague and the assistance you've been able to give, and you may return to your ordinary activities, and the court officer will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, can I raise a matter now that is unrelated to any particular next witness, but we've received an indication of a -- one of -- a possible problem which would arise because The Tribunal is not able to function next Tuesday, and that is that a witness, Aleksandric, is intended to be called on Monday but must finish on Monday and cannot wait until Wednesday when we would next sit. Are you able to indicate whether the half an hour that has been designated as the time that might be taken with the witness is reliable?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We expect to be very short with this witness. In fact, all the documents that are attached to his statement have already been agreed upon by the parties. So it's going to be just a matter of making him available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic, are you in a position to indicate how long cross-examination might be with the witness Aleksandric?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That's a very difficult question, but certainly if the examination-in-chief would last half an hour, the cross-examination would not then last the whole day. We shall probably have sufficient time to finish with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Djurdjic. I think in those circumstances we should plan to hear the witness Aleksandric commencing Monday morning, and we will clearly have to finish the witness in the course of Monday, so counsel should be very conscious of time accordingly. Now, are you dealing with the next witness, Ms. Kravetz? You're not. Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, it's my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Behar, there was a matter, was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I did just want to briefly address that I'm going to be seeking to make use of a map that's not yet in evidence, and as such I'm seeking to add that map to our 65 ter exhibit list and to make use of it today. I can indicate that the map is 65 ter number 05242. The map is essentially a close-up that's showing the region that Mr. Halimi [Realtime transcript read in error "Halilovic"] will testify about today. We recently obtained that map, and it's a much more detailed map of the area than any of the maps we currently had on our exhibit list. In my submission, it will make things clearer for the Chamber when Mr. Halimi explains what he saw. I can also indicate that it has been disclosed to the Defence, and I did speak to my learned friend briefly about it again this morning. I am not sure as to what position my learned friend is taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any objection, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had said back in the break to Mrs. Kravetz that I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very grateful. You may refer to the map, although it is not yet on the Rule 65 ter list. In fact you would like to move that it be added to your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be so ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and I thank my friend as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your full name and your date of birth for the record?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Mahmut Halimi. I was born on the 7th of April, 1954.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand that you were a judge for many years in Mitrovica later on -- first in the municipal court then later on in the District Court and that you later maintained your own private law practice. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And what kind of work are you currently doing?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I am a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what city you were living in in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I was living in Mitrovica, which is now after the war referred to as Northern Mitrovica, the part I lived in, on Ceta e Minatoreve Street, number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Halimi, did you testify at the Milutinovic et al trial on the 9th of October, 2006?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. To be honest, I don't remember the date when I testified, but it is true. I did testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Have you had a chance as well to listen to your testimony from that trial?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And I understand that there are two things in the transcript that you'd like to clarify or explain so that it accurately reflects your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could have up on the screen 65 ter number 05134. That's Mr. Halimi's testimony in Milutinovic et al. I'll need page 4506.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: At line 8 I see that it reads: "First of all, all Mitrovica and the witnesses that we heard knew that Nenad Pavicevic, Boban, and others involved were never members of the police in that police station in Mitrovica." I understand that you wanted to clarify that passage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. A wrong conclusion has been drawn because at the time and I remember this very well, I said the opposite, that everybody, including me, knew that Nenad Pavicevic, Boban and others were members of the police station in Mitrovica. They were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So is it fair to say then that would that passage would be more accurate just without the word "never," just for clarity?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. The word never should be removed, because everybody knows that from 1990 Boban, Nenad, who I know very well were policemen at the police station in Mitrovica. Everybody in Mitrovica knows that. I see that it's a mistake here on the transcript, but I already made the clarification. It is true that they were members on the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but I have learnt from you that the LiveNote, especially when the session is over, cannot be corrected in this way. I understand that the witness may have something new to say about the circumstances later, but I don't believe this technique of correcting the transcript once it's done is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you may have misunderstood the import of the question which is at lines 23 and 24: "It is not understood by me as suggesting that the record be changed. It was being put that it would be accurate if it were read without the word 'never' to clarify the meaning." So we will be leaving the transcript exactly as it is, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't mean to say that you were wrong, I was just reacting to the action of the Prosecutor and the way he wanted to correct an alleged mistake in the transcript. I had no objection to your interpretation. It's just that at the beginning of the trial you taught me how the transcript should properly be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic, but I think we can rely on what Mr. Behar is asking now as the way to understand correctly the evidence that is intended by Mr. Halimi.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Could we next have page 4510 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, from lines 14 to 18 on the screen you refer to soldiers that you saw along the road: " ... at the village of Runik in the correction of Rakosh. You then said that there were telephone land-line cables up to the village of Vitak. Is there something that you would like to clarify about this passage as well?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Again it has been recorded erroneously on the record. I said the following: From Vitak village up to the second village there were army forces on the left side of the road from Mitrovica to Peje, and by the asphalt road there were telephone cables up to Runik where from Runik to Rakosh there were soldiers at the centre of Runik. There were also policemen, police units, but at the exit up to Rakosh there were army forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And with those two things now mentioned, does this transcript accurately reflect your evidence and would you testify to these same facts today?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would then seek to tender 65 ter number 05134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00499, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I can now provide a brief summary of Mr. Halimi's evidence. I can indicate that it relates to paragraph 72(F) 73 and 77 of the indictment. Mr. Halimi is a Kosovar Albanian male from the village of Zhabar Mitrovica municipality. Prior to the breakout of the conflict, he worked as a judge at the District Court of Mitrovica and later began practising as a lawyer. Mr. Halimi describes the murder of two prominent Kosovo Albanians in Mitrovica, Latif Berisha and Agim Hajrizi shortly after the NATO air campaign began. On the 25th of March, 1999, Mr. Halimi received a phone call warning him that he needed to escape or he would be killed. He and his family left for the village of Zhabar and then spent six nights in the mountains before eventually returning. On the 15th of April, 1999, Mr. Halimi and his family observed Serb police and military units pushing approximately 25.000 to 30.000 people from neighbourhoods of Mitrovica towards Zhabar. Serb forces eventually split this crowd into two groups. The following morning these civilians were sent away towards the town of Peje. That same morning, Serb forces entered Zhabar firing their weapons and burning homes. On 17th of April, 1999, Mr. Halimi and his family joined a column of vehicles, that column travelled from Mitrovica to Klina then to Djakovica then past the town of Prizren into the border with Albania. Mr. Halimi describes the plight of the civilians during their deportation. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, I'm going to have a few questions for you today in order to clarify certain matters. I'm just going to focus on particular areas in light of the brief time we have. You explained in your earlier testimony that Asim Hajrizi was killed on the night of the 24th and the 25th of March, 1999. Can you explain to us who Mr. Hajrizi was?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Before I start, I would like to make a correction to ask for a correction to be made. My name is recorded on this transcript as Halilovic my name is Mahmut Halimi, not Halilovic as it is recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm sure we can have that corrected.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: As far as your question is concerned, Agim Hajrizi, I knew him very well, especially in the 1990s when as a representative of the trade union of the Battery factory in Mitrovica, I represented the 204 -- 240 workers to fight for their rights. Here my cooperation with Agim Hajrizi started, and I believe I assisted them as well in resolving the disputes of these workers that he represented as the chairman of the trade union of this factory in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was your sense of why he was killed? Your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Because of his activity that he was carrying out at the time in the interest of his people, in the interest of his colleagues who had remained without jobs because of the Milosevic regime. I would also like to point out that 1.240 workers had not received their salaries for a long period and their salaries were stolen by -- by the Serbian regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You described in your previous testimony that Latif Berisha was a professor at the University of Pristina and chairman of the LDK or the Democratic League of Kosovo. Can you tell us what happened to Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: He was executed in an identical manner for identical reasons because of his activity in Mitrovica and the surrounding areas of Mitrovica. He was the chairman of the Democratic League of Kosova branch in Mitrovica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You described in your previous testimony as well that on the 25th of March, 1999, at about 6.00 a.m. you received a telephone call from a woman speaking Serbian telling you to leave your home soon as possible, and you explain and this is at page 4445 of the transcript, that you then left your house. Can you explain what you understood that telephone call to mean?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: This was a message implying that my life was at -- at risk, that I was going to suffer the same fate as the two persons we mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And -- and just briefly, what was your understanding of why you were being targeted?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: From the 1990s up to the beginning of war, I was well known for my activities regionally in Mitrovica and in the whole territory of Kosova as one of the Albanians who opposed the Serbian regime, Milosevic regime, by practising as a lawyer and defending the interests and the rights of people, and because of my confrontations with the Serbian judiciary authorities while I was defending the interests of my clients.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about the observations that you made on the 15th of April, 1999. I'm going to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Could the usher please bring up 65 ter number 05242. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And perhaps if Mr. Halimi could be provided with a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, could you indicate roughly the location of the house that you were located in on the 15th of April on this map?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: First of all, I'm kind of handicapped here. I don't have my glasses with me, but I'll do my best. If you can zoom in a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I ask, Mr. Halimi, are your glasses in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they're not. I -- I left them at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know that I can help you very much then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe someone -- I can borrow them from someone if it's a plus 2 prescription.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know that we have any volunteers with the right glasses. I'm looking at the time and wondering whether a break would enable something to be done to enable Mr. Halimi to see the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be a good time for a break, and we'll certainly see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know where he is staying, but if it's nearby, it should be managed in the break. What we'll do is to adjourn now. We're just a little early, but we'll have the second break now and resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I see you're wearing glasses now, so hopefully we'll have a little more luck with the map. Just to go back again, you described at page 4449 of your previous transcript, moving to Upper Zhabar in a house that was above the rest of the village. Can you indicate on the map what was roughly the location of that house?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: The question arose earlier where my house was in the northern part, and I went to the Lower Zhabar, and I think you're asking a different question which has to do with me going from the Lower to the Upper Zhabar. Is that what you're interested in at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: At this point here should be where my house in the northern part of the town is located. I followed this route. It is the village of Suvi Do. Then I crossed into the stadium area. You can see the stadium there where I'm putting those dots. And I pursued the road up to Lower Zhabar where I stayed for two days. On the third day, in the middle of the night, I proceeded onto the Upper Zhabar, and I stayed near the Grmova mountain, which is in the vicinity, and in the company of a large number of my co-citizens from Mitrovica, most of them intellectuals from the town. That's where we went and stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, if you could -- could you put a number 1 by the location where you marked Lower Zhabar and a number 2 by the location where you marked the house you were in in Upper Zhabar.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You also described that from that location where you were in Upper Zhabar that you could see part of Mitrovica and Tavnik. Can you indicate where that area would be on the map and perhaps put a 3.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Tavnik is around here, number 3. Shipol can be seen here at number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally if you could indicate the road from Mitrovica to Peje, which you also discussed in your previous statement. If you could mark that with a 5 if you see it here.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: This is the road to Peje, which continues where the word Shipol can be seen, and from there onwards it goes out of Mitrovica in the direction of Peje. So it continues further down in the direction of Peje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 4450 of your previous transcript you describe the population moving en masse in Zhabar, and you also said that people were coming from the direction of Suhodol and from Tavnik. Can you indicate on the map where people were coming from and where they were going to?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I think it was on the 14th of April at about 10.00 when a massive movement of the population was observed. They were first coming from the direction of Tavnik and towards Zhabar, and from Shipol I can't see the village of Vinarce here, which is down here further down, Vaganica village, further down, and from Vaganica and Shipol in the middle of the fields and secondary roads and lanes. I think there was a large, an unprecedented influx of people who came from all those directions towards Zhabar. At the same time from Suhodol there were a large number of people who crossed the Ibar River towards Zhabar. At the same time, residents who had no vehicles at their disposal, had no cars, no trucks and so on, so they came on foot from Gusevac and Vinarce. They joined together and they crossed the river into the direction of Zhabar. This movement continued until half past 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. Zhabar and its environments, according to my best guesstimate, is about a hundred square kilometres. I can't be very precise there, but it's a very large village. And there was no room to swing a cat in. There was so many people over there all congregated in the fields, meadows, the yards of the private houses. It was a huge number of people. So by half past 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon. An overall number of no fewer than 35.000 people were there. A bit later in the course of the day, we heard some shooting exactly in that part of the town. A car which was on the left side in a feel was set fire to and burnt down. And at that stage we were able to observe a movement of the population to Shipol. There are two roads leading to Shipol one is in the vicinity of the school of Zhabar which continues perpendicular -- in a perpendicular direction to the Shipol school, whilst the other one it's a semicircular type of a road which goes from the main highway, the Adriatic highway towards Gatere [phoen], as we call it, which is a complex for timber-works. And then the road takes a left before going towards the Shipol school. The cars, tractors, big lorries join the column towards the convoys that join the convoy in this direction, in this perpendicular road which you can see above number 4. 4 is Shipol, 5 is the road towards Peje. Whereas the road that can be seen underneath the word Zhabar is the Adriatic highway I mentioned. So from here towards Shipol is the point which was occupied by the pedestrians. The convoy of vehicles, with the fall of night, was so big that the last one was by the Adriatic highway, and that is where they spent the whole night. At dawn or round about 7.00 or just a bit later maybe, from where I was in the upper Zhabar where you can see the Grmova mountain, point number 2, I was at some altitude, I think halfway to the top of this mountain. And from that vantage point, I was able to observe part of the road from Mitrovica to Peje, the whole of Zhabar, with the exception of the Shipol school, which could not be seen from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, let me -- let me -- pardon me. Let me just stop you there for a moment. We do have much of this from your previous testimony, and I know we're somewhat short of time. If we can pick up somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In fact perhaps before I do that could I ask that this map be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In your previous testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00500, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In your previous testimony, sir, you described the Serb forces burning houses in the lower part of Upper Zhabar on the 16th of April, and you described that you decided to leave, setting out in three cars with your family, and this is at page 4455. You describe spending that night in a carpentry compound and that then on the 17th of April, the police came and ordered you to make a column and to leave town. What I want to ask you, sir, is where this column that you were in went from there. I'm going to show you another map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter number 00001. This is The Times map of the Western Balkans. If we could have that zoomed in to show Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps while we're waiting for that, I'll just ask you another brief question about the route; and I know I'm jumping ahead a little bit, but when you were travelling in the convoy you described that you saw Serb forces. You described that you saw army, and you also described police. Do you remember what the police were wearing that you saw along the route?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: From Mitrovica, namely upon leaving Shipol to join the Peje road, the whole area was patrolled by regular police who had -- who had camouflage uniforms with a dominant blue colour, and they were on both sides of the road at the water-supply unit. However, I'm under the impression that there were special forces -- Special Police Units of the special forces on both -- on both sides. They had automatic shot, automatic weapons. They were wearing balaclavas, and they observed each and every single person who was part of the convoy be it on foot or in their own vehicles. So police were deployed along the road from the village of Brabonjic to Lubovec, again on both sides of the road. I can -- I cannot speak in terms of numbers because they were deployed in large numbers. There were also police on top of the hill in front of the village of Dubovec at some high point on the left-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just if you could describe then what these police that you saw were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: The ones who were by the water-supply unit were wearing a darker shade of uniform, again with the blue -- more predominant blue into black, as far as I can recall. And that is why I had the impression that they were members of the Special Police Unit who I had often seen in different parts of Mitrovica or Kosova as part of my daily duties at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just have the map zoomed in perhaps one more click. Thank you. Sir, could you just very briefly indicate the route that you followed in the convoy that you described in your previous testimony? And I don't know if we need to zoom in one more stage or are you able to see the names of the towns there?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I think I can. This is the Mitrovica-Peje road. We went up to Djurakovc, which means we did not enter Skenderaj, which you can see here, Runik, Djurakovc, the Belo Pole villages is a bit on the side of this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Perhaps it's easier just if you draw a solid line along the route you took if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Then I went this way exiting Klina towards Gjakove, and from Gjakove we went to Prizren, and then Zhur should be round about here. Dragash, Recan I can see. This bit here up to Prizren. Would you be able to zoom in a little bit more so I'd be able to see the village of Zhur? Would we also be able to see -- get this map a little bit higher so we'd be able to see the border point of Morine where we crossed the border point into Albania? Could you lift up the map a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, electronically we can't do that without losing the marking that you have already made. So we must leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's the road in the direction of Dragash. There it is. I've seen it now, sorry. That's where Kukes is. I lost it for a bit, but, yes, that is the road that we followed on our way to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours I would seek to tender that marked map as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, there are just two brief areas I want to ask you about. You indicated in your previous testimony that there were mosques in Mitrovica -- oh, sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked version, Your Honours, will be P00501.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, let me just ask you. Can you just tell me how many mosques there were in Mitrovica prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. There were four mosques. Three have been rebuilt after the war, whilst the fourth one, which is next to the western bridge above the Ibar River, has now been -- has now been covered up and on -- it was never rebuilt. The bridge was built in its stead or on its remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Before you left town on the 25th of March in 1999, were these mosques damaged?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And after you had left town, did you receive any information about those mosques?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were burnt down and destroyed whilst I was still in the Mitrovica region. However, I was not someone who could be described as an eye-witness. I did not observe them being destroyed. I learned of it later after returning from Albania to Mitrovica, i.e., that it was done by various Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Do you recall who you heard that from?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: There were a number of people who saw the flames, who saw it being set fire to, the ones who were hiding around the town of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You also indicated previously that you returned to Mitrovica on the 11th of July, 1999. When you returned, did you personally make any observations of those mosques?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: They were -- they'd all been destroyed. They'd been burnt down. And whilst the one who was beyond the Ibar River on the right-hand side did not exist any further. It had been covered up with earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And just one final question or, really, clarification. You explained earlier today that when you were working as a lawyer in the 1990s you had confrontations with the judicial authorities. You also explained in your previous testimony, this is at page 4472, that Albanian lawyers knew that they had to bribe Serbian bodies during these times and that you yourself had been involved in that practice. Can you explain to us why that would be and how the system was working in this time?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. It is well known even in Serbia, even honest citizens of Serbia know it. It was almost a public secret that Albanians had to pay for everything. Just imagine, Your Honours, that a citizen of Mitrovica had to pay 10 Deutschmarks to obtain a document, like a birth certificate, that he or she was entitled to. And we're talking here about passports, IDs, let alone other more substantial mass before a court of law. So we're talking about the system which in addition to being repressive it's also corrupt. Serbian regime did not have to resort to local Serbs to carry out the repression. They had to bring them from all over Serbia. They brought judges from all over the place and brought them into Mitrovica into local and Municipal Courts in Kosova with one and only one goal, to grab as much money as possible. I mentioned it earlier, and I'm reiterating it. This is the judicial system as it was reduced to where a judge at the local court would send -- would send a can of petrol to the clients, i.e., the lawyers who had -- who had to return before him to hear a case on the morrow. So what did he do? He left an empty can at their offices with the assumption that he was going to get it full in an hour or so, and again on the understanding that this was to do with someone who was going to appear before this very judge on the morrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Those are my questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Behar. Mr. Djurdjic, I think we've got 12 minutes. We ought to make some use of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halimi, my name is Veljko Djurdjic, member of the Defence team for the accused, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, and Mr. Alexander Popovic next to me is also a member of the team. I have a couple of questions for you. If there is any question you don't understand, do not hesitate to indicate so and I will try to rephrase. And please answer me only inasmuch as you can from your direct knowledge about things that you eye-witnessed personally, and since you are yourself a judge and a legal professional, you know exactly what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to call up Exhibit 500, P500. It's 0052. That's the map with markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We can use it if you wish. You will make new markings and then we will admit it under a new number. Could you encircle the urban area of Mitrovica, please? Just a moment. The legal officer will find a clear map.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: On the northern part the town of Mitrovica and [indiscernible] the Muslim cemetery. From there onwards we go north-east towards --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it goes to the village of Sipkovc. In blue here you can see the Trepco compound, which is the car battery industry, the petrol chemicals, and the zinc processing plant, which is now a case that has been closed. And it joins this part where you can see the stadium. Roughly this is the area of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood correctly, this is the central urban area of Mitrovica. And now would you mark the broader area of Mitrovica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: The municipal area now that Zvecan has become a separate municipality, is to be covered by this area, the line that I'm drawing now. It just goes beyond the Ibar River --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Halimi. I'm asking you about the time of 1999, not about today. Please mark the territory of the municipality as it was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Okay. This is the correct line. Let me go back to what it was like in 1999 and is roughly the same today because I did mention that towards the year of 1993, and 1994 Zubin Potok and Zvecan became separate municipalities which did no longer belong with the Mitrovica municipality. This all shows Mitrovica region, Reka, Lisica. This is Zvecan, and this is where the Mitrovica municipal area is. Everything that you can see southwards under the red line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would also like you to mark it on the south side. Start from the west and make a full circle around the Mitrovica municipality on the part of the map that we can see.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Forgive me, but at the very -- at the very end is Brabonjic which is the last village that belongs to the Mitrovica municipal area. The Ljushta, Vaganica, Svinjere, they all belong to Mitrovica. There are a number other villages which cannot be seen in this map. Svinjere is where the Vushtrri municipality boundary is. There are some villages here which belong to the Vushtrri community: Cucuivogel [phoen], Skupkovc, Zasella. There is quite a bit on the right-hand side which is the eastern part. There are number of villages like Zasajoc [phoen] which can be seen here up to Shalla e Bajgores, Zioca [phoen] and a number of other mountainous villages in the Shalla e Bajgores area which cannot be seen in this map, and I mean to say the eastern part of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halimi. You don't have to name the places. Just mark that broader circle on this map that encompasses the area of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand the witness to be saying that the borderline is beyond the edge of the map, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, yes, but on this map I still want to get these markings so that we can see certain distances in scale. If he can at least put a dotted line marking the boundary on one side and on the other side, and the south side as well, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let me delete that bit then. It goes fourth down in the south where it you can Brabonjic. That is the line that shows the end of the region of Mitrovica. And then adjacent to it is the Skenderi municipality with its own villages. There are number of villages here which cannot be seen in this map and further south. And then on the eastern side, about 16 or 22 kilometres, there are a number of villages up to -- which border the Podujevo municipality. They all belong to the Mitrovica region, but they cannot be seen in this map. The map, i.e., does not show the whole region of Mitrovica. That's why I can't explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Halimi, in this central urban part could you mark your house with an X.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Somewhere here it should be. Fifty metres from the main road that takes you to Zvecan. At that stage it was called Marsal Tito then Kral Petar I.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But I see two dots here. Is that a mistake or?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: It was maybe when I started drawing. This one here is the incorrect one. It should be the other one. Because I can see the Ceta e Minatoreve road that leads upwards. Forgive me. Just give me a second, please. It's somewhere there. If I were to see this map in some more detail, I'd be able to pinpoint it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I agree. It's a very small inconvenient map. Could you now mark the place in Donji Zabar where you were?

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: My brother's house is somewhere one the first ones adjacent to the stadium, about a kilometre away. It should be somewhere here in the vicinity of Ibar River which can be seen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you put a number 1 on it.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you mark the place where you were in Gornji Zabar with number 2.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The place where you were in Sipolje. Mark it with 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I did not say that I was in Shipol. I said I only was in Shipol when we left as part of that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you mark the school in Sipolje with number 3.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: I would have been able to do it were the map to show a bit more detail. It should be about a hundred metres from the Mitrovica-Peje road. So it should be somewhere here. So it's not adjacent. It's about a hundred metres away. So the second dot that I've made that show it a bit more precisely. The school of Shipol, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you put a number 3 there.

utterances.speaker: MAHMUT HALIMI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this map. I don't think we have any more time today, Your Honour. I will continue, with your leave, tomorrow with this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00065, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It is just past our time as you indicated, Mr. Djurdjic. I'm afraid, Mr. Halimi, we have to adjourn now because another trial is in the courtroom this afternoon. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.00, and we will ask you to return then. The court officer will assist you after we leave with closer directions. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 27th day of March, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 25
